synopsis: Pretoria independently verifies mining collision-avoidance systems under South Africa’s MOSH regime through staged laboratory tests followed by representative-mine trials, with brake robots and high-precision GPS used in the protocol [f15795, f1244, f6372]. Across 189 tests, reported pass rates were 62% for detection devices, 42% for machine-side systems and 83% for third-party interfaces; testing ran at 1.6 tests per week with an 18-week lead time as of October 2025, creating a constraint on a four-month schedule [f5178, f5180, f15809]. Hexagon’s Vehicle Intervention System reportedly passed Pretoria TRL4 verification in March 2026 before integrated site testing, but the cited vendor release provides no numbers [f1665, f6373]. Pretoria’s 2024 research links conservative collision-avoidance systems and false interventions to production losses, wear and resistance to adoption; steering-rate sampling aims to reduce those interventions, but its initial results are simulation-only [f15803, f6331]. MineSim, published in April 2025, is an open-source, peer-reviewed simulation system for autonomous open-pit trucks, incorporating scenarios from two real mines and mining-specific features such as unstructured roads and heavy-truck response lag [f464, f465, f466]. It demonstrates that mining-specific closed-loop scenario and planning simulation is feasible, not that sensor physics is validated; the booklet identifies sensor models in dust, snow and fog as an unresolved gap [f15808, f15810].
